description: The life of the Buddha, the Four Sights, the Dhamma, and the Three Marks of Existence.
content_html:
The Life of the Buddha

The Buddha was born as Siddhattha Gotama, a prince of the Shakya clan in what is now southern Nepal, traditionally around the fifth century BCE. His father, King Suddhodana, shielded him from the hardships of ordinary life, surrounding him with pleasure and luxury inside the palace walls. Yet, according to Buddhist tradition, the young prince was destined to seek a deeper truth.

The turning point came when Siddhattha ventured outside the palace on four separate occasions and encountered the Four Sights. He saw an old man, a sick man, a corpse and finally a wandering holy man who appeared at peace. These encounters shattered his sheltered worldview and revealed the universal reality of suffering. Siddhattha resolved to abandon his royal life and seek liberation.

Key Fact

The Four Sights—an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic—convinced Siddhattha Gotama to renounce his princely life and seek an end to suffering. The fourth sight showed that a path of spiritual seeking was possible.

After years of extreme asceticism proved fruitless, Siddhattha sat beneath a Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, vowing not to rise until he had found the truth. According to Buddhist tradition, he was tempted by Mara, the force of craving, desire and fear. The defeat of Mara in this encounter symbolises the overcoming of the three poisons—greed, hatred and delusion—that bind beings to the cycle of rebirth. At dawn, Siddhattha attained Enlightenment, becoming the Buddha (the ‘Awakened One’). He had reached Nibbana—the blowing out of craving, hatred and delusion.

The Dhamma

After his Enlightenment, the Buddha did not remain silent. He chose to share what he had discovered, and his first teaching—the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (recorded in Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)—was delivered to five former companions at the Deer Park at Sarnath. This discourse set out the Middle Way, avoiding extremes of self-indulgence and self-mortification, and presented the Four Noble Truths.

The word Dhamma (Sanskrit: Dharma) carries two connected meanings. First, it refers to the eternal law or truth that governs existence—the way things actually are. Second, it refers to the body of the Buddha’s teachings that reveal and explain that truth. Buddhists take refuge in the Dhamma as one of the Three Jewels (also called the Three Refuges): the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha (the community of practitioners). These three form the bedrock of Buddhist life.

Buddhism is not monolithic. The two principal branches—Theravada (‘Way of the Elders’) and Mahayana (‘Great Vehicle’)—both revere the Dhamma but emphasise different aspects. Theravada Buddhists, prevalent in South-East Asia, focus on the Pali Canon (the Tipitaka) as the authoritative record of the Buddha’s teachings. They emphasise the individual path to Nibbana through personal discipline and meditation.

Mahayana Buddhists, prevalent in East Asia and Tibet, have a broader canon that includes later sutras. They understand the Dhamma as encompassing not just the historical Buddha’s words but the eternal truth accessible through many enlightened beings (Bodhisattvas). This leads to a wider understanding of how the Dhamma can be taught and received. Both traditions agree that the Dhamma describes the nature of reality and the path to liberation.

Dependent Origination

Dependent origination (also called conditionality or paticca-samuppada) is one of the most important insights of the Buddha’s Enlightenment. It teaches that everything that exists arises because of causes and conditions. Nothing in the universe exists independently or by itself. When the conditions for something cease, that thing ceases too. The formula is often expressed as: “When this is, that is. From the arising of this comes the arising of that. When this isn’t, that isn’t.”

Dependent origination is described in detail through the 12 links (nidanas), which map out how one condition leads to the next across three lifetimes: past, present and future. The chain begins with ignorance (avijja), which gives rise to mental formations, consciousness, mind-body, the six senses, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and finally ageing and death. The Tibetan Wheel of Life illustrates this chain pictorially, showing how beings cycle through existence driven by these conditions. Crucially, because suffering arises from conditions, it can also cease when those conditions are removed—this is the logical basis for the Third and Fourth Noble Truths.

The Three Marks of Existence

The Buddha identified three universal characteristics of all conditioned existence. These are known as the Three Marks of Existence. Understanding them deeply is considered essential for liberation.

Key Fact

The Three Marks of Existence are: Dukkha (suffering/unsatisfactoriness), Anicca (impermanence), and Anatta (no fixed self or soul). Everything that is conditioned shares these three marks. The Dhammapada (verses 35–36) warns that the mind is hard to control and that bringing it under discipline leads to happiness.

Dukkha is commonly translated as ‘suffering’ but its meaning is richer. It includes obvious physical pain, the dissatisfaction of pleasant things ending, and the all-pervasive unsatisfactoriness underlying even neutral experiences. All conditioned things are dukkha because they cannot provide lasting, permanent satisfaction.

Anicca (impermanence) means that nothing conditioned lasts forever. Every physical object, every thought, every emotion, every relationship is subject to change and eventual ending. Buddhists believe that clinging to impermanent things is a primary cause of suffering, since we try to hold onto what cannot be held.

Anatta (no-self) is perhaps the most distinctive and challenging of the Buddhist teachings. It holds that what we call ‘the self’ is not a fixed, permanent, independent entity. Instead, what we think of as ‘I’ is a constantly changing process—a flow of physical form, feelings, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness (the five khandas). There is no unchanging soul or ‘atman’ (unlike Hindu teaching) that passes from life to life.

Theravada Buddhism emphasises anatta as the rejection of any permanent self, linking it directly to the five aggregates. Mahayana Buddhism extends this with the concept of sunyata (emptiness)—the idea that all phenomena, not just the self, lack inherent, independent existence. Both traditions agree that misunderstanding the self is the root of craving and therefore of suffering. The significance of anatta for Buddhists is profound: letting go of the false belief in a permanent self is central to the path to liberation.

The Buddha’s Importance Today

For Buddhists, the historical Buddha’s significance goes beyond biography. He is the exemplar—the one who proved that liberation from suffering is possible for a human being. His teachings (the Dhamma) provide the map, and his life provides proof that the journey can be completed. The Anguttara Nikaya (3.38) records the Buddha saying that he teaches one thing and one thing only: ‘suffering and the ending of suffering.’ This focus keeps the tradition practical and grounded in human experience rather than abstract theology.
exam_tip_html: When an ‘Outline’ question asks you to describe the Three Marks of Existence, name all three—Dukkha, Anicca, Anatta—and give a brief explanation of each. Simply naming them without explaining what they mean will limit your marks. For ‘Explain’ questions, always connect the concept to its significance for Buddhists: for example, understanding Anicca helps explain why clinging causes suffering. The 15-mark ‘Discuss’ question rewards balanced argument—explore both why a concept such as Anatta is central to Buddhism and why some students of religion find it challenging or unusual. Accurate spelling of technical terms such as ‘Nibbana’, ‘Anicca’ and ‘Anatta’ is rewarded in your extended response.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Siddhattha Gotama became the Buddha after the Four Sights prompted him to renounce palace life; he attained Enlightenment (Nibbana) after defeating Mara beneath the Bodhi tree, then taught the Dhamma at Sarnath.
  • The Dhamma is both the eternal truth of reality and the Buddha’s teachings that explain it; it is one of the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha) central to all Buddhist practice.
  • The Three Marks of Existence—Dukkha (suffering), Anicca (impermanence) and Anatta (no fixed self)—describe the nature of all conditioned existence; dependent origination explains how these conditions link together across the cycle of samsara.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term ‘Nibbana’ in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of the following: the end of suffering / the extinguishing of craving, hatred and delusion / the ultimate goal of Buddhist practice / the state the Buddha reached at Enlightenment. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the Four Sights that led Siddhattha Gotama to renounce his princely life.
practice_questions.marks: Students should describe the four encounters: an old man (showing the reality of old age), a sick man (showing the reality of illness), a corpse (showing the reality of death), and a wandering ascetic/holy man (suggesting that a spiritual path exists). 1 mark: naming two or more sights correctly. 2 marks: describing all four with a brief explanation of their significance. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline the Three Marks of Existence in Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per Mark of Existence, each requiring a name plus a brief explanation:
• Dukkha—suffering or unsatisfactoriness; all conditioned existence is unsatisfying.
• Anicca—impermanence; all conditioned things change and cannot last.
• Anatta—no fixed self; there is no permanent, independent soul.
[3 marks, 1 per correctly outlined Mark]

practice_questions.text:
Explain how the teaching of dependent origination is connected to the Buddhist understanding of samsara.
Refer to Buddhist teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Dependent origination (paticca-samuppada) teaches that everything arises from conditions—including rebirth. Because ignorance conditions mental formations, and so on through the 12 nidanas, beings are caught in the cycle of birth, ageing and death (samsara).
• The 12 links map how ignorance in a past life gives rise, through a chain of conditions, to a present life, which in turn conditions future existence.
• The Tibetan Wheel of Life illustrates how beings cycle through existence driven by the three poisons at the hub of the wheel.
• Because samsara is conditioned by ignorance and craving, it can cease when those conditions are removed, showing the path to liberation is logically possible.
• The Anguttara Nikaya 3.38 records the Buddha as teaching that he only teaches suffering and its ending, which dependent origination makes possible.
Mastering: both the logic of conditionality and its link to samsara are explained clearly with named teaching references and explicit analysis of the relationship.
Secure: conditionality and samsara are connected with a named reference and some development.
Developing: a basic link made between dependent origination and rebirth with limited development.
Emerging: a simple point about dependent origination or samsara with no clear connection. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'The most important thing the Buddha taught was that there is no permanent self.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Anatta (no fixed self) is unique to Buddhism and challenges the widespread human assumption that a permanent ‘I’ exists. If the belief in a permanent self is the root of craving, then understanding anatta is the key to ending all suffering.
• Theravada Buddhism teaches that the five khandas (aggregates) are what people mistake for a ‘self’, and seeing through this illusion is essential for Nibbana.
• The Dhammapada (35–36) links controlling the mind—which includes the illusion of self—to liberation. Without anatta, the Buddhist path makes less logical sense.
• Mahayana Buddhism extends this with sunyata, suggesting that emptiness of self is fundamental to all Buddhist metaphysics.

Arguments against or offering a different priority:
• The Four Noble Truths could be seen as the most important teaching: they provide the overall diagnosis (dukkha), cause (tanha), cure (Nibbana) and method (the Eightfold Path), of which anatta is just one supporting idea.
• The Dhamma itself—and specifically dependent origination (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)—might be considered the most important, as it explains why anatta is true; anatta follows from conditionality.
• For many lay Buddhists, the Five Precepts and ethical practice are the most practically important teachings in daily life.
• Theravada and Mahayana interpret anatta somewhat differently; some Mahayana schools speak of a ‘buddha-nature’ that complicates a straightforward ‘no-self’ reading, suggesting the teaching is more nuanced than the statement implies.

Mastering: both sides fully developed with named sources (Dhammapada 35–36, Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, reference to Theravada/Mahayana distinction), explicit weighing of arguments and a justified conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered with at least one named source and a clear conclusion.
Developing: some argument on both sides but limited use of sources and a weak conclusion.
Emerging: one-sided response with no sources and little or no conclusion. [15 marks, SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Describe the importance of the Dhamma as one of the Three Jewels of Buddhism.
practice_questions.marks: Students should identify that the Three Jewels are the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, and explain the significance of the Dhamma: it represents both the eternal truth and the Buddha’s teachings; Buddhists take refuge in the Dhamma as their guide to liberation. 1 mark: identifying the Dhamma as one of the Three Jewels. 2 marks: explaining its significance as both truth and teaching that guides Buddhists toward Nibbana. [2 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: What were the Four Sights that led Siddhattha Gotama to renounce his princely life?
options: A river, a forest, a palace and a marketplace
An old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering ascetic
A teacher, a monk, a king and a beggar

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the Three Marks of Existence?
The Three Jewels of Buddhism are the Buddha, the Dhamma and the _____.
The Buddhist teaching that nothing exists independently and that all things arise from conditions is called _____ origination.
Match each Pali term to its meaning:
right: The extinguishing of craving; the ultimate goal

flashcard_questions.q: What were the Four Sights that prompted Siddhattha to seek liberation?
flashcard_questions.a: An old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic.
The extinguishing of craving, hatred and delusion; the ultimate goal of Buddhist practice.

flashcard_questions.q: Who or what is Mara in Buddhist teaching?
flashcard_questions.a: The embodiment of temptation and distraction that tried to prevent Siddhattha's Enlightenment.
Both the eternal truth of reality and the Buddha's teachings that reveal it.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the Three Jewels of Buddhism?
flashcard_questions.a: The Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha.

flashcard_questions.q: What teaching does Samyutta Nikaya 56.11 record?
flashcard_questions.a: The Buddha's first formal sermon at Sarnath, setting out the Middle Way and Four Noble Truths.
Impermanence — the teaching that all conditioned things change and cannot last.
No fixed self — there is no permanent, independent soul in Buddhist teaching.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Dukkha as a Mark of Existence?
flashcard_questions.a: The unsatisfactory or suffering nature of all conditioned existence.

flashcard_questions.q: How many links (nidanas) are in the chain of dependent origination?
flashcard_questions.a: Twelve — beginning with ignorance and ending with ageing and death.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Tibetan Wheel of Life illustrate?
flashcard_questions.a: The 12 nidanas, showing how beings cycle through samsara driven by conditions.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Dhammapada (verses 35–36) say about the mind?
flashcard_questions.a: The mind is hard to control, but disciplining it leads to happiness and liberation.

glossary_terms.definition: Siddhattha Gotama, the historical founder of Buddhism, who attained Enlightenment and taught the way to the end of suffering.
The four encounters — an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering ascetic — that convinced the young prince to seek an end to suffering.
The embodiment of temptation and distraction in Buddhist teaching, who tried to prevent Siddhattha from reaching Enlightenment.
The state of perfect insight and liberation from suffering; the goal of Buddhist practice, meaning 'awakening'.
The cessation of suffering and the extinguishing of craving; the ultimate goal in Buddhism, called Nirvana in Sanskrit.
The first formal teaching given by the Buddha after his Enlightenment, sometimes called the 'Setting in Motion of the Wheel of the Dhamma'.
The teachings of the Buddha, and the eternal truths or laws that underpin reality; one of the Three Jewels of Buddhism.
The Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha — the three foundations of Buddhist faith and practice.
The Buddhist teaching that all phenomena arise in dependence upon conditions; nothing exists independently or permanently.
The twelve links or stages in the chain of dependent origination, showing how ignorance leads through a sequence of conditions to birth, ageing and death across multiple lifetimes.
The first Mark of Existence: the unsatisfactory, imperfect or suffering nature of conditioned existence.
The second Mark of Existence: the teaching that all conditioned things are impermanent and constantly changing.
The third Mark of Existence: the teaching that there is no fixed, permanent, independent self or soul.
